atoms.title: Kinematics — describing motion
atoms.summary: Position, velocity, and acceleration are the three layers of motion, each the time-derivative of the one before.

depths.eli5: Imagine watching a toy car. Three simple questions describe its motion: Where is it right now? How fast is it going? And is its speed changing? 'Position' is just where something is. 'Velocity' is how fast it moves and in which direction. 'Acceleration' is how quickly that velocity is changing — speeding up, slowing down, or turning. Kinematics is the part of physics that only describes motion; it never yet asks why the car moves.
depths.core: Kinematics describes how things move without yet asking what causes the motion (that 'why' is dynamics, covered later). A 'rate of change' means how fast one quantity changes as another (here, time) changes — in calculus this is called a derivative. Velocity is the rate of change of position over time; acceleration is the rate of change of velocity over time. When acceleration is constant, these relations can be added up (integrated) into the familiar formulas v = v₀ + at (speed grows steadily) and x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at² (position).
depths.deep: Velocity and acceleration are vectors — quantities that carry both a size and a direction (see the Vectors atom). Because direction counts, an object moving in a circle at constant speed is still accelerating: its speed (magnitude) is unchanged but its direction is constantly turning, so the velocity vector changes. Motion along a curved path (curvilinear motion) is where treating these quantities as full vectors stops being optional.

atoms.note: Constant speed is not the same as constant velocity: 'speed' is just the number, 'velocity' includes direction, so turning at a steady speed is still acceleration.

quiz.prompt: How are velocity and acceleration related to position?
quiz.answer: Velocity is the first time-derivative of position; acceleration is the first time-derivative of velocity (the second of position).

quiz.prompt: A car drives around a roundabout at a steady 30 km/h. Is it accelerating?
quiz.answer: Yes — its speed is constant but its velocity vector keeps changing direction, so there is a centripetal acceleration pointing toward the center.

atoms.title: Vectors and the dot/cross product
atoms.summary: Physical quantities with direction are vectors; the dot product measures alignment and the cross product measures perpendicular twist.

depths.eli5: Think of an arrow drawn on paper: it has a length and it points somewhere. That is a 'vector' — a quantity with both a size and a direction. Plain numbers (like temperature) have no direction; vectors do. There are two ways to 'multiply' two arrows. The dot product is a single number that tells you how much the two arrows point the same way (biggest when they line up, zero when they're at a right angle). The cross product makes a brand-new arrow that sticks straight out sideways from both of them.
depths.core: Force, velocity, and field are vectors — quantities with direction — not just plain numbers (which physicists call scalars). The angle between two vectors is θ (the Greek letter 'theta'). The dot product a·b = ab cosθ measures how aligned they are and produces a scalar; for example, work equals force·displacement (only the part of the force along the motion counts). The cross product a×b produces a new vector perpendicular (at a right angle) to both, with size ab sinθ; for example, torque (twisting effort) equals r×F. Here cos and sin are the cosine and sine functions from trigonometry.
depths.deep: The cross product is special to three-dimensional space and is antisymmetric — swapping the order flips the sign (a×b = −b×a). This is why 'right-hand rules' (point your fingers one way, your thumb gives the result's direction) appear everywhere in magnetism and rotation. In higher dimensions the true generalization is the wedge product, or equivalently an antisymmetric tensor (a more general directional object).

atoms.art_prompt: two arrows from a shared origin, a shaded projection of one onto the other, and a third arrow rising perpendicular out of their plane

quiz.prompt: Which product gives a scalar and which gives a vector, and what does each measure?
quiz.answer: The dot product gives a scalar measuring alignment (ab cosθ); the cross product gives a perpendicular vector measuring the twist between them (ab sinθ).

quiz.prompt: When are a·b and |a×b| each zero for nonzero vectors?
quiz.answer: a·b = 0 when the vectors are perpendicular; |a×b| = 0 when they are parallel (or antiparallel).

atoms.title: Derivatives and integrals for physics
atoms.summary: Differentiation extracts rates of change and integration accumulates them; physics is written almost entirely in this language.

depths.eli5: Two ideas power almost all of physics. A 'derivative' answers: how fast is something changing at this exact instant? (Like a car's speedometer reading right now.) An 'integral' does the opposite: it adds up countless tiny pieces to get a total. (Like adding up every tiny bit of distance to get the whole trip.) The neat part: they undo each other, the way adding and subtracting do.
depths.core: A 'differential equation' is a rule written in terms of how fast things change (their rates) rather than the answer directly. Nearly every physical law is a differential equation, and solving it means integrating — adding up the rates to find the actual quantity. The fundamental theorem of calculus is the bridge: if you integrate the derivative (rate of change) of something across an interval, you get back the net change of that something over the interval.
depths.deep: Vector calculus extends these ideas to fields — quantities defined at every point in space (like temperature in a room, or the electric field). The spatial derivatives are the gradient (which way a quantity increases fastest), divergence (how much a field spreads out from a point), and curl (how much it swirls around a point). Stokes' theorem and the divergence theorem are the multidimensional versions of the fundamental theorem, and they are exactly the machinery Maxwell's equations of electromagnetism are written in.

atoms.art_prompt: a curve with a tangent-line slope marked at one point and the shaded area beneath it, linked by a two-way arrow

quiz.prompt: What does the fundamental theorem of calculus say connects derivatives and integrals?
quiz.answer: Integrating the derivative of a function over an interval returns the net change of the function across that interval.

quiz.prompt: Explain to a beginner why most laws of physics are differential equations.
quiz.answer: Because nature specifies how a quantity changes from instant to instant (its rate) rather than handing you the answer directly; integrating those local rules reconstructs the global motion or field.

atoms.title: Newton's three laws of motion
atoms.summary: Inertia, F = ma, and action–reaction together turn forces into predicted motion.

depths.eli5: Three simple rules explain almost all everyday motion. (1) Things keep doing what they're doing — sitting still or coasting in a straight line — unless something pushes or pulls them. That tendency is called inertia. (2) A push changes an object's motion: a stronger push changes it more, and a heavier object changes less. (3) Every push comes with an equal push back the other way — when you push on a wall, the wall pushes on you.
depths.core: A 'force' is a push or pull; the 'net force' is the total once all pushes and pulls are added as vectors. First law: with no net force, velocity stays constant (this property is inertia, and frames of reference where it holds are called inertial frames). Second law: net force equals the rate of change of momentum, F = dp/dt, where momentum p = mv (mass times velocity); for constant mass this simplifies to the famous F = ma (force = mass × acceleration). Third law: forces always come in equal-and-opposite pairs acting on two different bodies. Once you know the forces, these laws make the future motion fully predictable (deterministic).
depths.deep: The deep content is the second law's identification of force with dp/dt (the rate of change of momentum), which survives into Einstein's relativity even though momentum p there is no longer simply mv. The third law guarantees conservation of momentum for isolated systems — and, via Noether's theorem, that conservation is secretly a statement about the uniformity (homogeneity) of space: physics works the same here as over there.

atoms.note: Action and reaction act on different bodies, so they never cancel on the same object.

quiz.prompt: State Newton's second law in its momentum form and say when it reduces to F = ma.
quiz.answer: F = dp/dt; it reduces to F = ma when mass m is constant, so dp/dt = m·dv/dt = ma.

quiz.prompt: A rocket pushes exhaust backward. Which law explains its forward thrust, and on what does the reaction act?
quiz.answer: The third law: the rocket pushes gas backward and the gas pushes the rocket forward — the reaction acts on the rocket, not on the rocket itself in a self-canceling way.

atoms.title: Momentum and its conservation
atoms.summary: Total momentum of an isolated system is conserved — the cleanest bookkeeping tool for collisions.

depths.eli5: Momentum is a measure of 'how much motion' something has — mass times velocity (a heavy, fast thing has a lot). The big rule: in any crash where nothing outside is pushing on the group, the total momentum of everything involved is exactly the same right before and right after. It just gets shared around.
depths.core: An 'isolated system' is a group of objects with no outside (external) force acting on it. Because the objects' internal forces on each other cancel in Newton's third-law pairs (equal and opposite), the total momentum of an isolated system cannot change — it is 'conserved.' This is enormously useful: collisions become solvable even when the messy details of the forces during impact are unknown, because you only need the before and after states.
depths.deep: Conservation of momentum is the dynamical shadow of translational symmetry of space — the fact that physics is the same wherever you are — via Noether's theorem (every continuous symmetry has a matching conservation law). It also holds in relativity and quantum mechanics, with the relativistic momentum p = γmv (γ, 'gamma', is a speed-dependent stretch factor) replacing the simple mv.

atoms.art_prompt: two carts colliding on a frictionless track with before/after velocity arrows whose mass-weighted sum is visibly equal

quiz.prompt: Under what condition is total momentum conserved?
quiz.answer: When the net external force on the system is zero (an isolated system); internal forces cancel as third-law pairs.

quiz.prompt: Show that momentum conservation follows from Newton's second and third laws for two interacting bodies.
quiz.answer: F₁₂ = −F₂₁ (third law). Each force equals dp/dt of its body, so dp₁/dt + dp₂/dt = F₂₁ + F₁₂ = 0, hence d(p₁+p₂)/dt = 0 and total momentum is constant.

atoms.title: Work, kinetic energy, and the work–energy theorem
atoms.summary: The work a net force does on an object equals the change in its kinetic energy.

depths.eli5: When you push something and it moves, you give it 'energy of motion' (called kinetic energy). The harder you push and the farther it moves while you push, the faster it ends up going. 'Work,' in physics, is exactly this: a force acting over a distance.
depths.core: In physics, 'work' has a precise meaning: force applied along a distance. Formally it is the line integral of force along the path, W = ∫F·dr (adding up force times each tiny step of movement). Kinetic energy is the energy of motion, ½mv² (half of mass times speed squared). The work–energy theorem says the net work done on an object equals the change in its kinetic energy. This is powerful because it converts a force problem into an energy problem — often you can skip tracking the motion instant by instant.
depths.deep: Only the part (component) of a force that points along the direction of motion does work; a force at a right angle to the motion (like the magnetic force on a charge, or the centripetal force in circular motion) does zero work, so it changes direction but not speed. The theorem is exact and follows directly from integrating Newton's F = ma along the path.

atoms.art_prompt: a block sliding right with a force arrow along the path, its speed indicator growing as a shaded area of force-times-distance fills in

quiz.prompt: What does the work–energy theorem equate?
quiz.answer: The net work done on an object equals the change in its kinetic energy, W_net = Δ(½mv²).

quiz.prompt: Why does the tension in a string doing circular motion at constant speed do zero work?
quiz.answer: Tension points toward the center, perpendicular to the velocity (and displacement), so F·dr = 0 everywhere — no work, and kinetic energy stays constant.

atoms.title: Conservation of energy and potential energy
atoms.summary: For conservative forces, kinetic plus potential energy is constant, and the force is the downhill gradient of the potential.

depths.eli5: Energy is the universal 'currency' for making things happen. It moves between motion (kinetic energy) and stored-up forms like height or a stretched spring (potential energy), but the total amount stays fixed if nothing wastes it. And things naturally tend to roll 'downhill' — toward lower stored energy, like a ball rolling into a valley.
depths.core: Potential energy (U) is stored energy that depends on position — height in gravity, or stretch in a spring. A 'conservative force' is one whose work depends only on the start and end points, not the path taken; such a force can be written as F = −∇U, the (negative) gradient of a potential energy (the gradient ∇U points the way U increases fastest). For conservative forces, the total mechanical energy — kinetic K plus potential U — stays constant. Non-conservative forces like friction convert mechanical energy into heat, but the grand total energy (now including that thermal energy) is still conserved.
depths.deep: Conservation of energy is the shadow of time-translation symmetry — physics is the same today as tomorrow — again via Noether's theorem. Mathematically, F = −∇U holds exactly when the force field has zero 'curl' (no built-in swirl); only such curl-free force fields admit a potential energy.

atoms.note: F = −∇U: force points from high to low potential, the direction of steepest descent (the gradient ∇U points uphill, so the minus sign turns it downhill).
atoms.art_prompt: a ball oscillating in a valley-shaped potential well with kinetic and potential energy bars trading height while their sum stays level

quiz.prompt: What relation lets you derive a conservative force from its potential energy?
quiz.answer: F = −∇U: the force is minus the gradient of the potential energy, pointing toward lower potential.

quiz.prompt: A pendulum swings without friction. Where is kinetic energy maximal and where is potential energy maximal?
quiz.answer: Kinetic energy is maximal at the lowest point (fastest); potential energy is maximal at the highest points of the swing (momentarily at rest).

atoms.title: Rotational motion and angular momentum
atoms.summary: Rotation mirrors linear motion: torque replaces force, moment of inertia replaces mass, and angular momentum is conserved without external torque.

depths.eli5: Spinning motion has its own versions of the ideas from straight-line motion. Instead of a 'push' you have a 'twist' (called torque — what a wrench gives a bolt). Instead of 'heaviness' you have how spread-out the mass is from the spin axis. And just as a coasting object keeps coasting, a spinning thing keeps spinning the same way unless something twists it.
depths.core: Each idea from straight-line motion has a rotational partner. Torque τ = r×F (the twisting effect of a force applied at a distance r from the axis) is the analog of force. The moment of inertia I — the mass weighted by its distance² from the rotation axis — is the analog of mass; mass far from the axis resists spinning more. Angular momentum L = Iω (where ω, 'omega', is the spin rate) is the analog of momentum; it changes only when an external torque acts, so it is conserved for isolated systems. That is why a figure skater spins faster when pulling their arms in.
depths.deep: Angular momentum conservation reflects the rotational symmetry of space (physics looks the same in every direction) via Noether's theorem. Because the moment of inertia I depends on both the chosen axis and how the mass is distributed, rigid-body rotation is really a tensor relationship (L = Iω with I a matrix, not a single number), and the free rotation of an irregular object can be surprisingly complex.

atoms.art_prompt: a skater pulling arms inward, the spin arrow lengthening as the mass distribution contracts toward the axis

quiz.prompt: What are the rotational analogs of force and mass?
quiz.answer: Torque (τ = r×F) is the analog of force; moment of inertia I is the analog of mass.

quiz.prompt: Why does a spinning skater speed up when pulling in their arms?
quiz.answer: Pulling in arms lowers I; with no external torque L = Iω is conserved, so ω rises to compensate for the smaller I.

atoms.title: Newtonian gravitation
atoms.summary: Every mass attracts every other with a force falling off as the inverse square of distance.

depths.eli5: Every chunk of matter pulls on every other chunk — that pull is gravity. The pull gets weaker fast as things move apart: put them twice as far away and the pull becomes only a quarter as strong. (That 'square the distance' weakening is called an inverse-square law.)
depths.core: Newton's law of universal gravitation gives an attractive force proportional to m₁m₂/r² — the two masses multiplied, divided by the square of the distance r between them; G is the gravitational constant (a fixed number setting the strength). Because the force shrinks with the square of distance, it is called an 'inverse-square law.' This single law explains both falling apples and the orbits of planets, and combined with F = ma it reproduces Kepler's laws of planetary motion. The matching potential energy is U = −Gm₁m₂/r.
depths.deep: There are two notions of mass here: 'gravitational mass' (how strongly gravity pulls on you, in this law) and 'inertial mass' (how much you resist being pushed, in F = ma). Newton noticed they are exactly equal but had no explanation. Einstein later elevated this coincidence to the equivalence principle — the seed that grew into general relativity, his theory of gravity as curved spacetime.

quiz.prompt: How does gravitational force scale with distance between two masses?
quiz.answer: As the inverse square of the separation, F ∝ 1/r².

quiz.prompt: Explain why the same G-based law governs both a falling apple and the Moon's orbit.
quiz.answer: Both are responses to Earth's gravity; the apple accelerates straight down while the Moon, moving sideways, perpetually 'falls' around Earth — same inverse-square force, different initial velocity.

atoms.title: Lagrangian mechanics
atoms.equation: \dfrac{d}{dt}\dfrac{\partial L}{\partial \dot q} - \dfrac{\partial L}{\partial q} = 0,\quad L = T - V
atoms.summary: Reformulates mechanics in terms of energy (L = kinetic − potential) and generalized coordinates, replacing vector forces with the Euler–Lagrange equation.

depths.eli5: Newton's way of doing mechanics means tracking every push and pull as an arrow. There's a slicker way. You write down a single quantity — the motion-energy minus the stored-energy — and feed it into one master equation that grinds out how the system moves, in whatever variables are most convenient (an angle, a distance along a track, anything).
depths.core: Here T is the kinetic energy (energy of motion) and V is the potential energy (stored energy). The Lagrangian is their difference, L = T − V, expressed using 'generalized coordinates' q — any convenient set of variables describing the configuration (an angle, a length, etc.) — and their rates of change (q̇, 'q-dot'). Plugging L into the Euler–Lagrange equation produces the equations of motion in any coordinate system, automatically respecting constraints (like a bead stuck on a wire) and never requiring you to break forces into x/y/z components. It gives the same physics as Newton's laws but is far more flexible.
depths.deep: Each coordinate q that does not appear explicitly in L gives a conserved quantity ∂L/∂q̇ — a generalized 'momentum.' This is Noether's theorem in action: a symmetry (the Lagrangian not caring about that coordinate) produces a conservation law. Lagrangian mechanics is the framework where symmetry and conservation become two faces of one structure.

atoms.note: A coordinate missing from L (called a cyclic or ignorable coordinate) means its matching ('conjugate') momentum is conserved.

atoms.art_prompt: a bead on a curved wire with coordinate q marked along the wire, the path emerging from a T-minus-V expression rather than force arrows

quiz.prompt: What is the Lagrangian, and what equation generates the equations of motion from it?
quiz.answer: L = T − V (kinetic minus potential energy); the Euler–Lagrange equation d/dt(∂L/∂q̇) − ∂L/∂q = 0 generates the motion.

quiz.prompt: Why does a coordinate absent from L give a conservation law?
quiz.answer: If q is absent then ∂L/∂q = 0, so d/dt(∂L/∂q̇) = 0, meaning the conjugate momentum ∂L/∂q̇ is constant in time.

atoms.title: The principle of least action
atoms.summary: Nature follows the path that makes the action — the time-integral of the Lagrangian — stationary.

depths.eli5: Imagine every possible route something could take to get from where it starts to where it ends. Nature seems to 'pick' one special route: the one where a particular running total (called the 'action') sits at a tipping point — nudge the path slightly and the total barely changes. Amazingly, all the laws of motion fall out of this one demand.
depths.core: The 'action' S is a single number you get by adding up the Lagrangian L over the whole path through time: S = ∫L dt. Out of all imaginable paths between fixed start and end points, the real path is the one that makes S 'stationary' — meaning a tiny change in the path produces no first-order change in S (written δS = 0, where δ means 'a small variation'). Demanding this directly reproduces the Euler–Lagrange equations, so the principle of least action is the bedrock from which classical mechanics can be derived.
depths.deep: 'Least' is a loose name — the action is stationary, which can be a minimum or a saddle point (a tipping point that's neither highest nor lowest), not always a true minimum. This principle reaches far beyond ordinary mechanics: field theory, relativity, and — through Feynman's path-integral formulation — quantum mechanics are all action principles, making least action arguably the single deepest organizing idea in physics.

atoms.note: Stationary, not strictly minimal — the true path is a critical point (a tipping point) of the action, which may be a minimum or a saddle.

quiz.prompt: What quantity is made stationary in the principle of least action, and over what?
quiz.answer: The action S = ∫L dt is made stationary (δS = 0) over all paths between fixed endpoints in time.

quiz.prompt: Explain why 'least action' is a slightly misleading name.
quiz.answer: The true path makes the action stationary — a critical point — which can be a minimum or a saddle, not necessarily an absolute minimum.

atoms.title: Hamiltonian mechanics
atoms.equation: \dot q = \dfrac{\partial H}{\partial p},\quad \dot p = -\dfrac{\partial H}{\partial q}
atoms.summary: Recasts mechanics in terms of position and momentum, with energy H generating the flow through symmetric first-order equations.

depths.eli5: Here's yet another way to do mechanics. Instead of position and velocity, you track two things: where something is (position) and how much momentum it carries (mass times velocity). A single energy function then quietly tells you how both of these tick forward, one small step at a time.
depths.core: The Hamiltonian H(q,p) is built from the Lagrangian by a mathematical swap called a Legendre transform, and it usually just equals the total energy (kinetic T + potential V). It replaces the single second-order Euler–Lagrange equation (involving acceleration) with two first-order equations describing how position q and momentum p each change. The pair (q, p) lives in 'phase space' — a space whose axes are position and momentum. This clean, symmetric structure is the natural launchpad for both statistical mechanics and quantum mechanics.
depths.deep: As a system evolves, a blob of nearby states in phase space keeps the same volume even as it stretches and twists (Liouville's theorem) — a foundation of statistical mechanics. The 'Poisson bracket' relation {q,p} = 1 (a bookkeeping rule for how q and p interrelate) is exactly what gets 'quantized' — promoted — into the quantum commutator [x̂,p̂] = iℏ (the rule that position and momentum can't both be sharp). Hamiltonian mechanics is the classical skeleton on which quantum theory is built.

quiz.prompt: What variables does the Hamiltonian formulation use, and what does H usually represent?
quiz.answer: Position q and momentum p (phase space); H usually equals the total energy T + V.

quiz.prompt: What classical structure becomes the quantum commutator [x̂, p̂] = iℏ?
quiz.answer: The Poisson bracket {q, p} = 1; quantization replaces Poisson brackets with commutators times iℏ.

atoms.title: Simple harmonic motion
atoms.summary: Any system with a linear restoring force oscillates sinusoidally at a fixed natural frequency.

depths.eli5: Pull a spring and let go: it wobbles back and forth at its own steady rhythm. The surprising part is that the rhythm (how many wobbles per second) is the same whether you pulled it a little or a lot. A swinging pendulum and a vibrating guitar string do the same thing — this repeating back-and-forth is called oscillation.
depths.core: A 'restoring force' is one that always pushes a system back toward its resting point. When that force is proportional to how far you've moved (displacement x), written F = −kx (k is the stiffness, the minus sign means 'back toward home'), the motion is simple harmonic. The equation of motion becomes ẍ = −ω²x (ẍ, 'x-double-dot', is acceleration), whose solution is a smooth sine wave with angular frequency ω = √(k/m) — set by the stiffness k and mass m. Crucially the frequency does not depend on amplitude (how far you pulled) — the hallmark of harmonic motion. Energy sloshes back and forth between kinetic and potential.
depths.deep: Simple harmonic motion is universal because almost any smooth energy 'valley' looks like a parabola near its bottom (a fact from the Taylor expansion, which approximates curves by simple polynomials). So small wiggles of nearly anything are harmonic. That is why the harmonic oscillator is the single most reused model in all of physics — from vibrating molecules to quantum fields.

atoms.note: Frequency is amplitude-independent only while the restoring force stays linear (proportional to displacement); push too far and this breaks down.
atoms.art_prompt: a mass on a spring tracing a sine curve over time, with energy bars trading between kinetic and potential at each extreme

quiz.prompt: What condition on the force produces simple harmonic motion, and what is the resulting frequency for a mass-spring system?
quiz.answer: A restoring force proportional to displacement (F = −kx); the angular frequency is ω = √(k/m), independent of amplitude.

quiz.prompt: Explain why the harmonic oscillator shows up everywhere in physics.
quiz.answer: Near any potential minimum the potential is approximately quadratic, so small oscillations of almost any system reduce to SHM.

atoms.title: Waves and the wave equation
atoms.equation: \dfrac{\partial^2 y}{\partial t^2} = v^2\,\dfrac{\partial^2 y}{\partial x^2},\quad v=f\lambda
atoms.summary: A wave is a disturbance that propagates at speed v, obeying a second-order equation linking its curvature in space and time.

depths.eli5: Wiggle one end of a long rope and you'll see the wiggle travel down the rope. Here's the strange part: the shape moves all the way along, but the rope material itself just bobs up and down in place — nothing actually travels the length of the rope except the pattern. That moving pattern is a wave.
depths.core: The relationship between wave speed v, frequency f (wiggles per second), and wavelength λ (length of one wiggle) is v = fλ. The wave equation, ∂²y/∂t² = v²∂²y/∂x², is the rule the disturbance y obeys; the symbols ∂² are 'second derivatives,' here measuring how curved the wave is in time and in space. It allows traveling-wave solutions of any shape moving at speed v, plus pure sine-wave solutions. Because the equation is 'linear,' waves superpose — they pass right through one another, add up or cancel (interfere), and can form fixed standing-wave patterns on a bounded system like a guitar string.
depths.deep: Superposition lets any wave be broken down into a sum of simple sine waves — the technique called Fourier analysis. Remarkably the same wave equation governs sound, vibrating strings, and light; only the speed v and the meaning of y change. The first complication beyond this clean picture is dispersion — when the speed v depends on frequency, so different colors or pitches travel at different speeds and a pulse spreads out.

quiz.prompt: Write the relation between wave speed, frequency, and wavelength.
quiz.answer: v = fλ — speed equals frequency times wavelength.

quiz.prompt: Two identical waves meet crest-to-trough. What property of the wave equation explains the cancellation, and what is it called?
quiz.answer: Linearity allows superposition; the waves add and cancel — destructive interference.

atoms.title: Coulomb's law and the electric field
atoms.summary: Charges exert an inverse-square force on each other; the electric field is the force per unit charge that fills the space around them.

depths.eli5: Electric charge comes in two flavors, called positive and negative. Two of the same flavor push apart; opposite flavors pull together. (You feel this as static cling.) The push or pull gets weaker with the square of the distance — just like gravity, except gravity only ever pulls, while electricity can also push.
depths.core: 'Charge' (symbol q) is the property that makes particles feel electric forces. Coulomb's law gives the force between two point charges as proportional to q₁q₂/r² (the charges multiplied, over distance squared); the constant 1/4πε₀ sets the strength, where ε₀ ('epsilon-naught') is a fixed property of empty space. Rather than imagine charges reaching across empty space ('action at a distance'), we say each charge fills the space around it with an electric field E = F/q — the force a tiny test charge would feel per unit of its charge. Another charge q then feels force F = qE. The field is the bookkeeping device that makes electromagnetism 'local' (things act on their immediate neighborhood).
depths.deep: Coulomb's law and Newton's gravity share the same inverse-square form, which is exactly why both obey a 'Gauss law' (next atom). The crucial difference is sign: charge comes in two kinds, so electric fields from different charges can cancel — unlike gravity, which has only one (always-attractive) kind.

quiz.prompt: Define the electric field in terms of force.
quiz.answer: The electric field is the force per unit positive test charge, E = F/q; a charge q in the field feels F = qE.

quiz.prompt: How does the Coulomb force differ qualitatively from Newtonian gravity despite both being inverse-square?
quiz.answer: Charge has two signs, so the electric force can attract or repel and fields can cancel; gravity has one sign and only attracts.

atoms.title: Gauss's law
atoms.summary: The electric flux through any closed surface is proportional to the charge enclosed — Coulomb's law restated as a field divergence.

depths.eli5: Picture wrapping any closed bag around some electric charge and counting the field lines poking out through the bag's surface. The count depends only on how much charge is sealed inside — not on the bag's size or weird shape. Charge inside means lines coming out; no charge inside means whatever goes in comes back out.
depths.core: 'Electric flux' is a measure of how much electric field passes through a surface — roughly, the number of field lines crossing it. Gauss's law says the net flux through any closed surface equals the total charge enclosed, divided by ε₀. Its 'differential form,' ∇·E = ρ/ε₀, says the same thing point-by-point: the divergence of E (how much field spreads out from a point) is set by the local charge density ρ ('rho'). For symmetric charge arrangements (a sphere, a long wire, a flat sheet) Gauss's law lets you compute the field almost instantly.
depths.deep: Gauss's law is mathematically equivalent to Coulomb's inverse-square law but more general — it also holds for moving charges, and it is one of Maxwell's four equations of electromagnetism. Its very existence is a consequence of the 1/r² geometry of three-dimensional space (field lines from a point spread over a sphere whose area grows as r²).

atoms.art_prompt: a charge enclosed in an arbitrary blobby closed surface with field lines piercing it, the count independent of the surface shape

quiz.prompt: What does Gauss's law relate the electric flux through a closed surface to?
quiz.answer: To the total charge enclosed by that surface, divided by ε₀.

quiz.prompt: Sketch how Gauss's law gives the field of a point charge.
quiz.answer: By symmetry E is radial and constant on a sphere of radius r; flux = E·4πr² = q/ε₀, so E = q/(4πε₀r²) — Coulomb's law recovered.

atoms.title: Magnetic field and the Lorentz force
atoms.summary: A charge feels an electric force plus a velocity-dependent magnetic force perpendicular to both its motion and the field.

depths.eli5: A magnetic field (the invisible influence around a magnet) only affects a charge that is moving. And it shoves that charge sideways — never along its direction of travel, always at a right angle. Because the shove is always sideways, the charge curls around instead of speeding up or slowing down.
depths.core: The magnetic field is written B; the electric field is E; the charge's velocity is v. The Lorentz force law F = q(E + v×B) is the complete recipe for how electric and magnetic fields push on a charge q. The magnetic part, qv×B, uses the cross product (see the Vectors atom), so it points perpendicular to the velocity. A force at a right angle to motion does no work (no energy change), so it only bends the path — into a circle or a corkscrew (helix). In a deep sense, magnetism is just electricity viewed from a moving frame of reference.
depths.deep: Because the magnetic force does no work, magnetic fields can change a particle's direction but never its speed. Special relativity reveals E and B as two parts of one unified object (the electromagnetic field tensor): what one observer calls a purely magnetic effect, another observer moving past will partly describe as electric — they're the same thing seen from different motions.

atoms.note: The magnetic force never changes a particle's speed — only its direction.

atoms.art_prompt: a positive charge moving right through a field pointing into the page, curving upward along a circular arc with a perpendicular force arrow

quiz.prompt: Write the Lorentz force law and state why the magnetic part does no work.
quiz.answer: F = q(E + v×B); the magnetic force qv×B is perpendicular to v, so F·v = 0 and it does no work.

quiz.prompt: A charged particle enters a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to its velocity. What path does it follow and why?
quiz.answer: A circle — the magnetic force is constant in magnitude and always perpendicular to velocity, providing centripetal force without changing speed.

atoms.title: Faraday's law of induction
atoms.summary: A changing magnetic flux induces a circulating electric field — the principle behind generators and transformers.

depths.eli5: Move a magnet near a coil of wire and electricity starts to flow in the wire — no battery needed. The key is motion or change: a magnet just sitting still does nothing. It's the changing magnetic field that pushes the current. This is exactly how power plants generate electricity.
depths.core: 'Magnetic flux' (Φ_B) is the amount of magnetic field passing through a loop. An 'electromotive force' (EMF) is the voltage-like push that drives current around a circuit. Faraday's law says the EMF around a loop equals minus the rate at which the magnetic flux through it changes. The point-by-point (differential) form, ∇×E = −∂B/∂t, says a changing magnetic field creates a 'curling' electric field — one that loops around rather than pointing straight out from charges. The minus sign encodes Lenz's law: the induced effect always opposes the change that caused it.
depths.deep: This is the first crack in the static picture of electricity. Electric fields no longer come only from charges; they can also be born from changing magnetic fields, with field lines that form closed loops. Faraday's law is one of Maxwell's four equations and is half of the self-sustaining mechanism that makes light possible.

atoms.note: Lenz's law (the minus sign) is energy conservation in disguise: induced currents flow so as to oppose the change driving them.
atoms.art_prompt: a bar magnet plunging into a coil with an induced circulating current arrow and a curling electric field looping around the changing flux

quiz.prompt: What induces an electromotive force in a loop according to Faraday's law?
quiz.answer: A changing magnetic flux through the loop; the EMF equals minus the rate of change of that flux.

quiz.prompt: Explain the physical meaning of the minus sign in Faraday's law.
quiz.answer: It is Lenz's law: the induced current flows so as to oppose the change in flux, which is required by energy conservation.

atoms.title: Ampère–Maxwell law
atoms.summary: Currents and changing electric fields both create circulating magnetic fields — Maxwell's displacement-current fix completes the set.

depths.eli5: Two things make a magnetic field. First, an electric current (charges flowing through a wire) — known for centuries. Second, and surprisingly, a changing electric field, even in empty space with no wire at all. That second part, added by Maxwell, is what makes light possible.
depths.core: 'Circulation' of the magnetic field means how much it loops around a closed path. Ampère's original law tied that circulation to the electric current passing through (J is the current density). Maxwell noticed it broke down when charge piles up — like on a capacitor (two plates storing charge) being charged through a gap with no current crossing. He fixed it by adding the 'displacement current' term μ₀ε₀ ∂E/∂t (μ₀, 'mu-naught', is the magnetic counterpart of ε₀), which says a changing electric field acts like a current for making magnetic fields. With this addition the four Maxwell equations become complete and self-consistent.
depths.deep: The displacement current is the mirror-image partner of Faraday's law: a changing E makes B, just as a changing B makes E. This mutual feedback — each changing field regenerating the other — is exactly what lets self-sustaining electromagnetic waves travel through empty space.

atoms.note: The displacement-current term is what makes Maxwell's equations consistent with conservation of charge (charge is never created or destroyed).

quiz.prompt: What two things can create a circulating magnetic field according to the Ampère–Maxwell law?
quiz.answer: An electric current J and a changing electric field (the displacement current μ₀ε₀ ∂E/∂t).

quiz.prompt: Why did Maxwell need to add the displacement-current term?
quiz.answer: To make the law consistent when current is interrupted (e.g., between capacitor plates), preserving charge conservation and enabling EM waves.

atoms.title: Maxwell's equations unified
atoms.summary: Four equations fully specify how electric and magnetic fields are made by charges and currents and how they sustain each other.

depths.eli5: Just four rules describe everything about electricity and magnetism: where the fields come from and how they push each other around. The shocking bonus: put the four rules together and they predict that light exists and travels at one fixed speed.
depths.core: The four equations are: Gauss's law (electric charges are the sources of the electric field E); no magnetic monopoles (∇·B = 0 — magnetic field lines never start or stop, there are no isolated 'north poles'); Faraday's law (a changing magnetic field B creates a looping electric field E); and the Ampère–Maxwell law (currents and changing electric fields create a looping magnetic field B). Together they form a closed, self-contained system. From these four alone you can derive that the fields travel as waves at speed c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀) — and plugging in the measured constants gives exactly the speed of light.
depths.deep: That this speed c comes out of purely electric and magnetic constants — with no mention of any observer's motion — clashed head-on with the older Galilean idea that speeds should add. That contradiction is what pushed Einstein to special relativity. Remarkably, Maxwell's equations were already 'Lorentz-invariant' (they obey relativity's symmetry); it was Newton's mechanics that had to be corrected.

atoms.note: c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀): the speed of light is built from the electric constant ε₀ and magnetic constant μ₀ alone.
sources: Physics LibreTexts: Maxwell's Equations and Electromagnetic Waves
atoms.art_prompt: four field-line panels — diverging E from charge, looped B with no source, E curling around changing B, B curling around changing E — joined into one frame

quiz.prompt: What does ∇·B = 0 express physically?
quiz.answer: There are no magnetic monopoles; magnetic field lines have no sources or sinks and always close on themselves.

quiz.prompt: Where does the speed of light come from in Maxwell's framework?
quiz.answer: Combining Faraday's and Ampère–Maxwell's laws in vacuum yields a wave equation for E and B propagating at c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀).

atoms.title: Electromagnetic waves
atoms.summary: Oscillating electric and magnetic fields sustain each other and travel through vacuum at the speed of light.

depths.eli5: A changing electric field creates a magnetic field, which (as it changes) creates an electric field again, and so on — a ripple that keeps feeding itself as it races across empty space. That self-feeding ripple is light. Radio waves, visible light, and X-rays are all the same thing, just rippling faster or slower.
depths.core: Maxwell's equations in empty space (vacuum) give wave equations for the electric field E and magnetic field B, traveling at speed c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀). The fields are 'transverse' (they wiggle sideways, across the direction of travel), mutually perpendicular (E and B at right angles to each other and to the motion), and 'in phase' (they peak together). The wave carries both energy and momentum. Radio, visible light, and X-rays are the same phenomenon at different frequencies — the electromagnetic spectrum.
depths.deep: Electromagnetic waves need no medium to travel through — a historic shock that demolished the old idea of a 'luminiferous ether' filling space. The Poynting vector S = E×B/μ₀ tracks the direction and rate of energy flow, and because the wave carries momentum it exerts 'radiation pressure' — a real push of light, behind solar sails and the tails of comets pointing away from the Sun.

sources: Physics LibreTexts: Maxwell's Equations and Electromagnetic Waves

quiz.prompt: How are E, B, and the direction of propagation oriented in an EM wave?
quiz.answer: All three are mutually perpendicular; E and B oscillate in phase and are transverse to the propagation direction.

quiz.prompt: Explain to a beginner why light needs no medium to travel.
quiz.answer: The wave is a self-sustaining exchange between changing electric and magnetic fields; each regenerates the other, so it can propagate through pure vacuum.

atoms.title: Temperature and the zeroth/ideal-gas laws
atoms.summary: Temperature measures average molecular kinetic energy; the ideal-gas law links it to pressure and volume.

depths.eli5: Heat is really just tiny jiggling. The atoms in any object are always moving, and 'hotter' simply means they're jiggling faster on average. Squeeze a gas into a smaller space, or warm it up, and its molecules hit the walls harder and more often — that's higher pressure.
depths.core: 'Thermal equilibrium' means two things in contact have stopped exchanging net heat. The zeroth law of thermodynamics says objects in thermal equilibrium share one common number — their temperature T. 'Kinetic theory' (treating a gas as countless tiny bouncing molecules) identifies T with the average energy of molecular motion: ⟨½mv²⟩ = (3/2)k_BT, where k_B is Boltzmann's constant (the conversion factor between temperature and energy). The ideal-gas law PV = Nk_BT — linking pressure P, volume V, and number of molecules N — then follows from molecules drumming on the container walls.
depths.deep: A 'degree of freedom' is an independent way a molecule can hold energy (moving along x, y, z; spinning; vibrating). The equipartition theorem says each quadratic degree of freedom carries ½k_BT of energy on average, which connects the microscopic count of motions to a substance's bulk heat capacity. Even more fundamentally, temperature is defined through entropy: 1/T = ∂S/∂E (how much the disorder S grows per unit of added energy E) — the thermodynamic definition, beyond the kinetic picture.

atoms.note: Equipartition: ½k_BT of energy per quadratic degree of freedom — translation, rotation, and vibration each count as ways to store energy.
atoms.art_prompt: gas molecules bouncing in a box, faster arrows where it is hotter, hammering the walls to produce pressure

quiz.prompt: What microscopic quantity does temperature measure in an ideal gas?
quiz.answer: The average translational kinetic energy of the molecules, ⟨½mv²⟩ = (3/2)kT.

quiz.prompt: If you double the absolute temperature of a fixed amount of gas at constant volume, what happens to its pressure?
quiz.answer: It doubles — by PV = NkT, with N and V fixed, P is proportional to T.

atoms.title: First law of thermodynamics
atoms.summary: Energy conservation for thermal systems: internal energy changes by heat added minus work done by the system.

depths.eli5: There are two ways to add energy to something: heat it up, or do mechanical work on it (like squeezing or stirring). Either way, energy is never created or destroyed — it just moves around, between heat, work, and the energy stored inside the object.
depths.core: The first law of thermodynamics is conservation of energy with heat included. 'Internal energy' U is the total energy stored inside a system (all that molecular jiggling and bonding). U goes up when heat Q flows in and goes down when the system does work W on its surroundings (like a gas pushing a piston outward): dU = δQ − δW. Heat and work describe processes of transfer, not stored amounts — so they are not 'state functions.' Their combination, the change in internal energy dU, is a state function: it depends only on the start and end states.
depths.deep: δQ and δW are written with δ (not d) because they are 'inexact differentials' — their totals depend on the exact path taken between two states, while dU does not. This is precisely why you cannot store 'heat' inside an object; you can only store energy. Heat and work are merely two channels through which that energy gets transferred.

atoms.note: U is a state function (depends only on the current state); Q and W are path-dependent (depend on the route taken) — which is why we write δ, not d, for them.
atoms.art_prompt: a gas cylinder with heat flowing in from below and a piston doing work above, internal energy shown as a central reservoir level

quiz.prompt: State the first law of thermodynamics in words.
quiz.answer: The change in a system's internal energy equals the heat added to it minus the work it does on its surroundings.

quiz.prompt: Why do we write δQ and δW but dU?
quiz.answer: Heat and work depend on the process path (inexact differentials), whereas internal energy is a state function whose change depends only on endpoints.

atoms.title: Entropy and the second law
atoms.summary: Entropy never decreases in an isolated system — the arrow of time and the limit on engines.

depths.eli5: Things naturally tend to get more mixed-up and disordered, never spontaneously tidier. Stir milk into coffee and it blends — but it never un-blends on its own. That one-way tendency, true for the whole universe, is the second law of thermodynamics.
depths.core: 'Entropy' (S) is a measure of how spread-out and disordered the energy and matter of a system are. The second law says that any spontaneous (natural, unforced) process in an isolated system increases its total entropy; entropy stays exactly constant only for an idealized 'reversible' process (one that could run backward through the same states). 'Reversible' means perfectly slow and lossless. This law sets a hard ceiling on how efficient any heat engine can be, and it defines the 'arrow of time' — the reason the past and future feel different.
depths.deep: Thermodynamic temperature itself is defined through entropy: 1/T = ∂S/∂U (how much disorder grows per unit of added internal energy U). The second law is statistical, not an iron rule: violating it isn't strictly impossible, just overwhelmingly unlikely, because there are vastly more disordered (high-entropy) arrangements than orderly ones — the deeper reason explained by the Boltzmann atom that follows.

atoms.art_prompt: a partition removed between hot and cold gas, molecules mixing irreversibly into a uniform warm cloud with an entropy gauge climbing

quiz.prompt: What does the second law say about the entropy of an isolated system?
quiz.answer: It never decreases; it increases for irreversible processes and stays constant only for reversible ones.

quiz.prompt: Why can't a heat engine convert all absorbed heat into work?
quiz.answer: Doing so would lower total entropy; some heat must be dumped to a cold reservoir to keep ΔS ≥ 0, capping efficiency.

atoms.title: Boltzmann's entropy and the microscopic view
atoms.summary: Entropy counts microstates: it is Boltzmann's constant times the log of the number of ways a macrostate can be realized.

depths.eli5: Why does disorder win? Count the possibilities. There are a zillion ways for a deck of cards to be shuffled but only one way for it to be perfectly sorted. A state that can be arranged in a huge number of ways (that all look the same from the outside) has high entropy. Disorder is simply having many more indistinguishable options.
depths.core: A 'microstate' is one specific arrangement of all the molecules (exactly which atom is where, moving how). A 'macrostate' is the big-picture description you can actually see (temperature, pressure, total volume) — many microstates produce the same macrostate. Boltzmann connected entropy to counting: S = k_B ln Ω, where Ω ('omega') is the number of microstates that match a given macrostate, and ln is the natural logarithm (which keeps the gigantic counts manageable). This explains why entropy increases: a system naturally drifts toward macrostates that can be realized in vastly more ways, simply because there are more of them.
depths.deep: This formula is the bridge from microscopic mechanics to large-scale thermodynamics. The Boltzmann distribution and partition function (next atom) both follow from maximizing S subject to a fixed average energy. In a real sense, all of statistical mechanics is the systematic exploitation of S = k_B ln Ω.

atoms.note: Engraved on Boltzmann's tombstone: S = k log W (his W is the same as Ω, the microstate count).

atoms.art_prompt: a single macrostate label connected to a sprawling fan of countless microscopic arrangements, the count feeding a log into the entropy value

quiz.prompt: What does Ω represent in S = k ln Ω?
quiz.answer: The number of microstates (microscopic arrangements) consistent with the given macrostate.

quiz.prompt: Use S = k ln Ω to explain why entropy tends to increase.
quiz.answer: Macrostates with more microstates are vastly more numerous, so a system explores and ends up in high-Ω (high-entropy) macrostates simply by counting.

atoms.title: Boltzmann distribution and partition function
atoms.summary: In equilibrium the probability of a state falls exponentially with its energy, normalized by the partition function Z.

depths.eli5: Nature prefers low-energy states — like water settling to the bottom — but warmth gives things enough of a nudge to occasionally visit higher-energy states too. The hotter it is, the more often. If you tally up all those preferences into one grand sum, you get a quantity called Z that secretly contains all the answers.
depths.core: A 'heat bath' is a large surrounding environment that holds a system at a fixed temperature T. Such a system occupies a given state i with probability proportional to e^(−Eᵢ/k_BT) — the 'Boltzmann factor,' which shrinks exponentially as the state's energy Eᵢ rises (so high-energy states are rare, and rarer when cold). The 'partition function' Z is the sum of all these Boltzmann factors; it normalizes the probabilities so they add to 1. Once you know Z, you can extract every thermodynamic quantity (energy, entropy, free energy) just by taking derivatives. It is the central object of statistical mechanics.
depths.deep: The (Helmholtz) free energy is F = −k_BT ln Z, tying the microscopic sum directly to macroscopic thermodynamics. For independent parts of a system, Z multiplies (factorizes) — which is exactly why simple two-state and lattice models are so tractable. Here β ('beta') = 1/(k_BT) is a common shorthand for 'inverse temperature.'

atoms.note: Once you can write Z, you can compute everything: F = −k_BT ln Z, and the average energy ⟨E⟩ = −∂lnZ/∂β (where β = 1/k_BT).

quiz.prompt: What is the partition function and why is it central?
quiz.answer: Z = Σ e^(−Eᵢ/kT), the sum of Boltzmann factors; it normalizes probabilities and yields all thermodynamic quantities by differentiation.

quiz.prompt: Two states differ by energy ΔE at temperature T. What is their population ratio?
quiz.answer: p_high/p_low = e^(−ΔE/kT); a few kT of energy difference makes the higher state far rarer.

atoms.title: Geometric optics — reflection and refraction
atoms.summary: When wavelength is small, light travels in rays that reflect and bend at interfaces according to Snell's law.

depths.eli5: When you don't need to think about light as a wave, you can treat it as straight 'rays.' Rays travel in straight lines, bounce off mirrors at equal angles, and bend when they pass from air into water or glass. That bending is why a straw in a glass of water looks broken at the surface.
depths.core: When the wavelength is tiny compared to the objects involved, electromagnetic waves act like straight 'rays' — this is geometric optics. Reflection keeps the angle (angle in equals angle out). Refraction — the bending as light crosses a boundary — follows Snell's law, n₁sinθ₁ = n₂sinθ₂, where θ is the angle from the surface's perpendicular ('normal') and n is the 'refractive index,' equal to c/v (how much slower light travels in that material than in vacuum). Lenses and mirrors form images by exploiting these two rules.
depths.deep: Snell's law can be derived from Fermat's principle of least time — light takes the path that minimizes (more precisely, makes stationary) its travel time, itself a least-action principle for light — or from matching up the wave's crests at the boundary. When light tries to exit into a less-dense medium too steeply, there's no valid exit angle and it reflects entirely: 'total internal reflection,' the trick that traps light inside fiber-optic cables.

atoms.art_prompt: a light ray bending toward the normal as it passes from air into denser glass, with both angles measured from the surface normal

quiz.prompt: State Snell's law and define the refractive index.
quiz.answer: n₁sinθ₁ = n₂sinθ₂; the refractive index n = c/v is the ratio of light's vacuum speed to its speed in the medium.

quiz.prompt: What variational principle does Snell's law follow from?
quiz.answer: Fermat's principle of least time — light takes the path that makes its travel time stationary, which yields the sine relationship at an interface.

atoms.title: Wave optics — interference and diffraction
atoms.summary: Light's wave nature shows up as interference fringes and diffraction patterns when paths differ by whole wavelengths.

depths.eli5: Shine light through two tiny side-by-side slits onto a screen and you don't get two bright spots — you get a row of bright and dark stripes. Those stripes only make sense if light is a wave: where two waves' crests meet they brighten, where a crest meets a trough they cancel into darkness.
depths.core: 'Coherent' light sources are ones whose waves stay in lockstep. When light from two such sources overlaps, the difference in distance traveled determines the result: a path difference of a whole number of wavelengths means crests line up — 'constructive interference,' bright; a difference of a half-wavelength means crest meets trough — 'destructive interference,' dark. For two slits separated by distance d, bright fringes appear where d sinθ = mλ (m = 0, 1, 2, …). 'Diffraction' — the bending and spreading of waves around edges and through openings — blurs fine detail and so limits the resolution of any optical instrument.
depths.deep: Interference is the decisive classical evidence that light is a wave. Yet the very same double-slit setup fired one photon at a time still builds up the stripe pattern, revealing quantum superposition (each particle somehow goes 'both ways'). The diffraction limit, roughly λ/D for an aperture of size D, sets the ultimate resolving power of telescopes and microscopes — bigger lenses and shorter wavelengths see finer detail.

quiz.prompt: What is the condition for bright fringes in a two-slit interference pattern?
quiz.answer: d sinθ = mλ — the path difference between slits is a whole number of wavelengths.

quiz.prompt: Why did the double-slit experiment settle the wave-vs-particle debate for light (classically)?
quiz.answer: Interference fringes can only arise from waves adding and canceling; particles would simply pile up behind each slit with no alternating pattern.

atoms.title: Special relativity — postulates and Lorentz transforms
atoms.summary: Demanding the same speed of light for all observers warps space and time into Lorentz-mixed coordinates.

depths.eli5: No matter how fast you race toward a beam of light, you always measure it moving at the same speed — you can never gain on it. Strange as that is, experiments confirm it. The price for it being true: clocks that move relative to you tick slowly, and moving rulers shrink along their direction of motion.
depths.core: A 'frame of reference' is a point of view from which you measure positions and times; an 'inertial frame' is one moving at constant velocity (no acceleration). Einstein built relativity on two postulates: (1) the laws of physics are the same in every inertial frame, and (2) the speed of light c is the same for every observer, no matter their motion. The old 'Galilean' rule for adding velocities can't satisfy this; the 'Lorentz transformation' (the correct rule for converting one observer's space-and-time measurements to another's) does. Its consequences — time dilation (moving clocks run slow), length contraction (moving objects shorten), and relativity of simultaneity (observers disagree on what's 'at the same time') — are all scaled by the factor γ ('gamma'), which grows as speed approaches c.
depths.deep: The constancy of c isn't an arbitrary assumption — it's forced by Maxwell's equations, which already singled out no preferred frame. Lorentz transformations are precisely the symmetry that leaves Maxwell's equations unchanged; it was Newton's mechanics that had to be corrected to match.

atoms.note: γ ≈ 1 for everyday speeds (so relativity is invisible in daily life); its effects only become large as v approaches c, the speed of light.

quiz.prompt: State Einstein's two postulates of special relativity.
quiz.answer: (1) The laws of physics are identical in all inertial frames. (2) The speed of light in vacuum is the same for all inertial observers.

quiz.prompt: A muon travels at 0.99c. Qualitatively, why does it reach the ground despite its short lifetime?
quiz.answer: Time dilation (large γ) stretches its lifetime in the ground frame, so it survives the trip — equivalently, length contraction shortens the distance in the muon's frame.

atoms.title: Spacetime and the invariant interval
atoms.summary: Space and time merge into one four-dimensional geometry where the spacetime interval, not time alone, is absolute.

depths.eli5: Relativity reveals that time and space aren't really separate things — they're woven into one fabric called 'spacetime.' Two observers moving differently will disagree about how much time passed and how far apart two events were, but they will always agree on one combined 'spacetime distance' between the events.
depths.core: The mathematician Hermann Minkowski showed that Lorentz transformations are like rotations in a four-dimensional spacetime (three space dimensions plus time), but with a peculiar minus sign attached to the time part. The 'spacetime interval' Δs² combines the time and space gaps between two events, and it is 'invariant' — every observer computes the same value even while disagreeing on the separate time (Δt) and space (Δx) gaps. Cause and effect are encoded in the 'light cone' (the set of points a light flash could reach): only events close enough that something slower than light could travel between them ('timelike separated') can influence each other.
depths.deep: The 'metric signature' (−,+,+,+) — one minus sign for time, three pluses for space — is the whole story; it sorts every pair of events into timelike, spacelike, or lightlike separation. This geometric way of seeing relativity is the gateway to general relativity, where the flat Minkowski spacetime gets replaced by a curved, dynamic geometry that gravity bends.

quiz.prompt: What quantity is invariant for all inertial observers in special relativity?
quiz.answer: The spacetime interval Δs² = −c²Δt² + Δx² + Δy² + Δz², even though Δt and Δx individually differ between frames.

quiz.prompt: Explain what the light cone tells you about causality.
quiz.answer: Only events within (or on) each other's light cones are timelike/lightlike separated and can be causally connected; spacelike-separated events cannot influence one another.

atoms.title: Mass–energy equivalence
atoms.summary: Mass is a concentrated form of energy; a body at rest still holds energy E₀ = mc².

depths.eli5: Even an object sitting perfectly still carries a huge amount of hidden energy, locked up in its mass. Convert just a tiny sliver of that mass and you release an enormous amount of energy. That's exactly what powers nuclear reactors and makes the Sun shine.
depths.core: In relativity, a particle's total energy E, its momentum p, and its mass m are tied together by E² = (pc)² + (mc²)². For a body at rest (momentum p = 0) this collapses to the famous E₀ = mc² — its 'rest energy' is its mass times the speed of light squared. Because c² is a gigantic number, even a speck of mass equals a vast energy. So mass and energy are interconvertible: nuclear reactions release energy by turning a small 'mass deficit' into energy, and the energy binding a nucleus together literally makes it weigh slightly less.
depths.deep: The same relation shows that a massless particle (m = 0) still carries energy, E = pc, and is forced to travel at exactly c — that's what a photon (a particle of light) is. The rest mass m is the 'length' of the energy–momentum four-vector (a combined energy-and-momentum object in spacetime), and like the spacetime interval it is the same for all observers (Lorentz-invariant).

atoms.note: Massless particles obey E = pc and must move at exactly the speed of light c.
