quiz.prompt: Write the full energy–momentum relation and state what it gives for a particle at rest.
quiz.answer: E² = (pc)² + (mc²)²; at rest p = 0 so E₀ = mc².

quiz.prompt: What does the relation predict for a massless particle?
quiz.answer: With m = 0, E = pc, so it has energy and momentum but no rest mass and must travel at c — like a photon.

atoms.title: Equivalence principle
atoms.summary: Locally, gravity is indistinguishable from acceleration — the insight that turns gravity into geometry.

depths.eli5: Imagine you're inside a sealed box with no windows. Could you tell whether the box is resting on a planet (gravity pulling you down) or being accelerated upward through empty space by a rocket (the floor pushing up on you)? Einstein realized you couldn't — gravity and acceleration feel exactly the same from inside.
depths.core: Recall the two kinds of mass from the gravitation atom: 'gravitational mass' (how hard gravity pulls you) and 'inertial mass' (how hard you resist a push). Because they're equal, every object falls the same way regardless of its mass, and an observer in free fall feels no gravity at all (think of astronauts floating). Einstein's equivalence principle states that local physics in a uniform gravitational field is identical to physics in an accelerating frame. He called this his 'happiest thought,' and it reframes gravity not as a force but as a feature of moving through curved spacetime.
depths.deep: The principle holds only 'locally' — in a small enough region. Over a larger region, 'tidal effects' (the way a real gravitational field varies from place to place, e.g. pulling slightly inward toward a planet's center on both sides) show up and can't be erased by any single acceleration. Those leftover tidal forces are exactly what the curvature of spacetime encodes.

atoms.note: The equivalence is local: over any extended region, tidal forces (the field's variation from point to point) betray real spacetime curvature.
atoms.art_prompt: a person in an accelerating rocket and the same person standing on a planet, a dropped ball falling identically in both windowless cabins

quiz.prompt: What does the equivalence principle assert about gravity and acceleration?
quiz.answer: Locally, the effects of a uniform gravitational field are indistinguishable from those of an accelerating reference frame.

quiz.prompt: Why is the equivalence principle only valid locally?
quiz.answer: Over extended regions, tidal differences in a real gravitational field (e.g., field lines converging toward a planet) appear that no single acceleration can mimic — these reveal genuine spacetime curvature.

atoms.title: Curved spacetime and geodesics
atoms.summary: Free-falling bodies follow geodesics — the straightest possible paths through curved spacetime.

depths.eli5: Einstein's big idea: gravity isn't really a pulling force. It's the shape of spacetime itself. A heavy object like the Sun warps the spacetime around it, like a bowling ball denting a trampoline. Planets aren't being tugged — they're just rolling along the straightest possible path through that curved landscape.
depths.core: In general relativity, mass and energy curve spacetime, and an object in free fall traces a 'geodesic' — the curved-space version of a straight line (technically, the path that makes the elapsed 'proper time,' the time on the object's own clock, extremal). The 'Christoffel symbols' Γ ('Gamma') are the mathematical bookkeeping that captures how the geometry tilts these paths from point to point. What we perceive as a gravitational force is really just geodesic motion through curved geometry.
depths.deep: The geodesic equation is itself a least-action principle for curved spacetime: extremize the proper time ∫dτ ('integral of d-tau,' summing the object's own clock-ticks along the path). The full curvature of spacetime is captured by the 'Riemann tensor,' and 'geodesic deviation' — how two nearby free-falling paths drift together or apart — is the precise mathematical form of tidal gravity (the same tides from the equivalence-principle atom).

atoms.art_prompt: a massive body denting a spacetime grid while a smaller body rolls along the straightest available curved track around the well

quiz.prompt: What path does a freely falling body follow in general relativity?
quiz.answer: A geodesic — the straightest possible path (extremal proper time) through curved spacetime.

quiz.prompt: Explain how GR reinterprets the 'force' of gravity.
quiz.answer: There is no force; mass-energy curves spacetime, and free objects simply follow geodesics of that geometry, which we perceive as gravitational attraction.

atoms.title: Einstein field equation (a glimpse)
atoms.summary: Matter and energy tell spacetime how to curve; the curved spacetime tells matter how to move.

depths.eli5: All of gravity boils down to one master equation with a beautifully simple meaning: matter and energy tell spacetime how to bend, and bent spacetime tells matter how to move. Gravity is that two-way conversation between stuff and the shape of space and time.
depths.core: The Einstein field equation sets the 'Einstein curvature tensor' G_μν (a measure of how spacetime is curved, built from the geometry and its rates of change) proportional to the 'stress–energy tensor' T_μν (a single object packaging all the energy, momentum, and pressure of matter). The subscripts μ and ν ('mu' and 'nu') just label the four spacetime directions. Solving the equation for a given lump of matter gives you the spacetime geometry; geodesics (from the previous atom) in that geometry then dictate how things move. In the limit of weak gravity and slow speeds, it reproduces Newton's familiar law of gravity.
depths.deep: Written out, G_μν = R_μν − ½R g_μν (R is curvature, g_μν the 'metric' that defines distances). A 'cosmological constant' term Λg_μν (Λ, 'Lambda') can be added; it drives the observed acceleration of the universe's expansion. These are ten coupled nonlinear partial differential equations, and their famous solutions include black holes (the Schwarzschild solution), expanding universes (the FLRW models), and ripples in spacetime itself (gravitational waves), all since confirmed by observation.

atoms.note: Often written G_μν + Λg_μν = (8πG/c⁴)T_μν once the cosmological constant Λ is included.
atoms.art_prompt: a balance with the curvature tensor on one pan and a glowing energy-matter distribution on the other, spacetime grid bending in response

quiz.prompt: In one sentence, what does the Einstein field equation relate?
quiz.answer: It relates the curvature of spacetime (G_μν) to its energy–momentum content (T_μν), with proportionality 8πG/c⁴.

quiz.prompt: Name two famous classes of solutions to the Einstein field equation.
quiz.answer: The Schwarzschild solution (black holes / spherical masses) and the FLRW solutions (expanding/contracting cosmologies); gravitational waves are another.

atoms.title: Quantization — photons and the photoelectric effect
atoms.summary: Light energy comes in discrete quanta of size hν, the experimental crack that opened quantum mechanics.

depths.eli5: We usually picture light as a smooth continuous stream, but it actually arrives in tiny indivisible packets, like grains of sand. Each packet (a 'photon') carries a fixed amount of energy set by the light's color. Shine light on metal and only packets carrying enough energy can knock an electron loose — and brightness alone can't help if each packet is too weak.
depths.core: A 'quantum' (plural quanta) is a smallest indivisible chunk of something. The photoelectric effect — light knocking electrons out of a metal — showed that whether electrons fly off depends on the light's frequency (its color), not its intensity (brightness). This only makes sense if light energy comes in quanta of size E = hν, where ν ('nu') is the frequency and h is Planck's constant; each such quantum is a 'photon.' The 'work function' φ ('phi') is the minimum energy needed to free an electron; below it no electrons escape no matter how bright, and above it the freed electron's maximum kinetic energy is hν − φ.
depths.deep: This is 'wave–particle duality': light behaves as a wave (it interferes, from the wave-optics atom) yet also as a stream of particles (photons). Reconciling the two forced an entirely new mechanics — quantum mechanics. Planck's constant h is the fundamental 'quantum of action' (a tiny unit setting the scale of quantum effects); its extreme smallness is exactly why the graininess of energy is invisible in everyday life.

atoms.note: Planck's constant h is the quantum of action — it sets the size of the 'graininess' of the world.
atoms.art_prompt: discrete photon packets striking a metal surface, only those above a threshold energy knocking electrons free with leftover kinetic energy

quiz.prompt: What does the photoelectric effect reveal about light, and what equation captures a photon's energy?
quiz.answer: Light energy is quantized into photons of energy E = hν; ejection depends on frequency, not intensity.

quiz.prompt: Why does dim blue light eject electrons from a metal while bright red light may not?
quiz.answer: Each blue photon may exceed the work function φ while each red photon does not; intensity adds more photons but cannot raise a single photon's energy above threshold.

atoms.title: Matter waves — de Broglie
atoms.summary: Every particle has a wavelength inversely proportional to its momentum — matter is wavy too.

depths.eli5: Here's the flip side of the previous idea. If light (a wave) can act like particles, then particles (like electrons) can act like waves. Every moving object has a wavelength — a wiggle length — and the more momentum (mass times speed) it has, the shorter that wave.
depths.core: Louis de Broglie ('de Broy') proposed that any particle with momentum p has an associated wavelength λ = h/p, where h is Planck's constant. This bold guess was confirmed by 'electron diffraction': beams of electrons form interference fringe patterns, exactly like waves of light. It also explains where quantization comes from — only a whole number of these wavelengths can fit neatly around an atomic orbit (this is essentially Bohr's condition, covered in the Bohr-model atom).
depths.deep: For everyday objects the wavelength is unimaginably tiny because h is so minuscule and their momentum is huge — which is why you never see a thrown baseball diffract. The matter-wave idea demanded an equation to describe how these waves behave and evolve — Schrödinger's equation — and made the 'wavefunction' (the mathematical wave describing a particle) unavoidable.

atoms.art_prompt: a beam of electrons passing through a crystal lattice and forming a ring diffraction pattern, each electron drawn as a short wave packet

quiz.prompt: Write the de Broglie relation and say what it asserts.
quiz.answer: λ = h/p; every particle has a wavelength inversely proportional to its momentum.

quiz.prompt: Why don't we observe the wave nature of everyday objects?
quiz.answer: Their momenta are enormous compared to h, so λ = h/p is unimaginably small — far below any measurable or diffractable scale.

atoms.title: The wavefunction and Born rule
atoms.summary: A quantum system's complete state is a complex wavefunction whose squared magnitude gives the probability of measurement outcomes.

depths.eli5: Before you look, a quantum particle isn't simply 'here' or 'there.' Instead it's described by a spread-out wave covering many places at once. To find the odds of detecting it at any given spot, you take that wave's height there and square it. Bigger wave there means more likely to be found there.
depths.core: The 'wavefunction,' written ψ (the Greek letter 'psi'), is the complete mathematical description of a quantum system — it holds everything that can be known. The Born rule says that |ψ|² (the wave's magnitude, squared) at a location gives the 'probability density' — how likely a measurement is to find the particle there. Because the particle must be found somewhere, the total over all space must equal 1 (this is 'normalization'). A deep break from classical physics: quantum mechanics predicts only probabilities, not certain outcomes.
depths.deep: ψ is a 'complex' quantity — it carries a 'phase' (an angle, like the hand of a clock) in addition to a size. Phase has no everyday analog, but relative phases between parts of the wave produce interference, the hallmark of quantum behavior. When you measure, ψ appears to suddenly 'collapse' to a single definite state (an eigenstate) — the most mysterious and hotly debated part of the theory (the 'measurement problem').

atoms.note: The phase of ψ (its clock-hand angle) has no classical analog, but it is exactly what makes quantum interference possible.
atoms.art_prompt: a spread-out complex wave over a line with its squared-magnitude shaded as a probability hump, total shaded area equal to one

quiz.prompt: What does the Born rule say |ψ(x)|² represents?
quiz.answer: The probability density of finding the particle at position x upon measurement; integrating it over all space gives 1.

quiz.prompt: Why must the wavefunction be complex rather than real?
quiz.answer: Its phase carries physical information: relative phases between contributions produce interference, which real probabilities alone cannot encode.

atoms.title: Schrödinger equation
atoms.summary: The wavefunction evolves deterministically in time under the Hamiltonian — quantum mechanics' equation of motion.

depths.eli5: Just as Newton's F = ma tells an everyday object how to move, there's a master equation for the quantum world that tells the wavefunction how to ripple forward in time, given the energy landscape it sits in. That master equation is Schrödinger's.
depths.core: The Schrödinger equation governs how the wavefunction ψ changes over time. An 'operator' is a mathematical action performed on the wavefunction; the central one here is the Hamiltonian operator Ĥ ('H-hat'), which represents the system's total energy (kinetic + potential). Here ℏ ('h-bar') is Planck's constant divided by 2π, and i is the imaginary unit (√−1). For 'stationary states' (standing-wave patterns that don't change shape) the equation becomes an eigenvalue problem Ĥψ = Eψ, whose allowed solutions come only at certain discrete energies E — which is exactly why atoms have quantized energy levels.
depths.deep: The time evolution of ψ is fully deterministic and 'unitary' (it preserves total probability at 1); genuine randomness enters only at the moment of measurement. The kinetic-energy term −(ℏ²/2m)∇² arises from the rule p → −iℏ∇ — replacing classical momentum p with a derivative operator, the substitution that converts classical energy expressions into a quantum equation.

atoms.note: Evolution of ψ is deterministic and smooth; only the act of measurement injects probability.
atoms.art_prompt: a wavefunction in a potential well morphing smoothly over time, with standing-wave eigenstates at discrete energy levels picked out

quiz.prompt: What does the time-independent Schrödinger equation Ĥψ = Eψ determine?
quiz.answer: The stationary states and their allowed (often discrete) energy eigenvalues E for a given potential.

quiz.prompt: What operator replaces classical momentum p to build the Hamiltonian, and what kinetic term does it give?
quiz.answer: p → −iℏ∇, so p²/2m becomes −(ℏ²/2m)∇², the kinetic-energy operator in the Schrödinger equation.

atoms.title: Operators, observables, and eigenstates
atoms.summary: Every measurable quantity is a Hermitian operator; its eigenvalues are the possible measurement results.

depths.eli5: In quantum mechanics, anything you can measure — position, speed, energy — is represented by a kind of 'machine' (an operator) that acts on the wavefunction. Strangely, the only readings that machine can ever give you are its own special set of numbers, not just any value.
depths.core: An 'observable' is any measurable quantity (position, momentum, energy). Each is represented by a 'Hermitian operator' — a special, well-behaved kind of mathematical operator. An 'eigenvalue' is one of an operator's characteristic numbers, and the matching 'eigenstate' is the wave-pattern that goes with it. A measurement always returns one of these eigenvalues, and right after, the system is left in the corresponding eigenstate. The 'expectation value' ⟨A⟩ is the average result you'd get over many identical measurements on identically prepared systems.
depths.deep: Hermitian operators are used because they guarantee real (not imaginary) eigenvalues — which is necessary since real measurements give real numbers — and a complete set of orthogonal eigenstates (a usable 'basis'). Whether two observables can both be sharply known at once depends on whether their operators 'commute' (give the same result in either order). When they don't, you get an uncertainty relation — the algebraic root of Heisenberg's principle in the next atom.

atoms.note: Hermitian operators have real eigenvalues — exactly what measured quantities must be, since you never read off an imaginary number on an instrument.
atoms.art_prompt: an operator box acting on a wavefunction and returning one highlighted eigenstate with its eigenvalue read off a dial

quiz.prompt: What are the possible results of measuring an observable, in operator language?
quiz.answer: The eigenvalues of the (Hermitian) operator representing that observable.

quiz.prompt: Why must observables be represented by Hermitian operators?
quiz.answer: Because Hermitian operators have real eigenvalues (measurements are real numbers) and a complete orthogonal set of eigenstates.

atoms.title: Heisenberg uncertainty principle
atoms.summary: Position and momentum cannot both be sharply defined; pinning one blurs the other.

depths.eli5: There's a hard trade-off in the quantum world: the more precisely you know where a particle is, the less you can possibly know about how fast it's moving — and the reverse too. This isn't because our instruments are clumsy; it's a built-in feature of how reality works at the smallest scales.
depths.core: Δx ('delta-x') means the uncertainty (the spread) in position, and Δp the uncertainty in momentum. Because the position and momentum operators don't 'commute' (the order you apply them matters), their uncertainties must obey Δx·Δp ≥ ℏ/2 — squeeze one small and the other necessarily grows. This is a property of the wavefunction itself, traceable to a 'Fourier' relationship (any wave narrow in space is automatically made of a wide range of wavelengths, hence momenta). It is not about measurement clumsiness.
depths.deep: More generally, any two non-commuting observables A and B satisfy ΔA·ΔB ≥ ½|⟨[A,B]⟩|, where [A,B] is their 'commutator' (a measure of how much order matters). The energy–time version of this principle explains why short-lived unstable states have fuzzy (broadened) energies, and underlies the fleeting 'virtual particles' of quantum field theory.

atoms.note: It is fundamental, not instrumental — a consequence of the wave (Fourier) structure of matter itself.
atoms.art_prompt: a narrow position wave packet paired with its broad momentum spread, the two widths visibly trading off as one is squeezed

quiz.prompt: State the position–momentum uncertainty relation.
quiz.answer: Δx·Δp ≥ ℏ/2 — the product of position and momentum uncertainties has a fixed lower bound.

quiz.prompt: Explain why uncertainty is fundamental rather than a limitation of instruments.
quiz.answer: It follows from the Fourier relationship between a wave's spatial spread and its momentum spread; a state with sharp position must contain a wide range of momenta, regardless of how it is measured.

atoms.title: Quantum tunneling
atoms.summary: A particle can pass through an energy barrier it classically lacks the energy to cross.

depths.eli5: Picture a ball that doesn't have enough energy to roll over a hill — classically it's stuck. But a quantum particle can sometimes simply appear on the far side of a barrier it 'shouldn't' be able to cross. Its wave leaks into the barrier and occasionally pops out the other side. This is called tunneling.
depths.core: A 'potential barrier' is a region that costs more energy to be in than the particle has. Classically the particle bounces back. Quantum-mechanically, the wavefunction doesn't stop dead at the barrier — it decays exponentially (shrinks fast) inside, and if the barrier is thin enough, a bit of wave emerges on the far side with reduced amplitude, meaning a real chance of finding the particle there. The 'transmission probability' (chance of getting through) drops exponentially with the barrier's width and height: thin, low barriers are tunneled easily; thick, tall ones almost never.
depths.deep: Tunneling is not a curiosity — it runs the universe. It lets protons in stars fuse by sneaking through their mutual electric (Coulomb) repulsion; it causes radioactive alpha decay; and it is the working principle of the scanning tunneling microscope and of flash memory in your devices. It is one of the most direct, observable consequences of matter's wave nature.

atoms.art_prompt: a wavefunction hitting a tall barrier, decaying exponentially within it, and emerging as a small transmitted wave on the far side

quiz.prompt: What is quantum tunneling?
quiz.answer: The passage of a particle through a potential barrier higher than its energy, forbidden classically but allowed because the wavefunction penetrates and partially transmits.

quiz.prompt: How does the transmission probability depend on barrier width, and name one real application.
quiz.answer: It decays exponentially with width (T ~ e^(−2κL)); applications include stellar fusion, alpha decay, and scanning tunneling microscopy.

atoms.title: Spin and the Pauli exclusion principle
atoms.summary: Particles carry intrinsic angular momentum (spin); identical half-spin particles refuse to share a quantum state.

depths.eli5: Electrons behave like they have a tiny built-in magnet, called 'spin,' that can only point one of two ways — call them 'up' or 'down.' On top of that, no two electrons can ever be in the exact same state at the same place. That simple 'no-sharing' rule is what builds the whole periodic table of elements.
depths.core: 'Spin' is an intrinsic angular momentum — a built-in 'rotation-like' property with no true everyday analog (the particle isn't literally spinning). Electrons are 'spin-½,' meaning the spin measured along any axis can only be +ℏ/2 or −ℏ/2 (up or down). All particles split into two families: 'fermions' (half-integer spin, like electrons) and 'bosons' (integer spin, like photons). The Pauli exclusion principle forbids two identical fermions from sharing the same quantum state. This is why electrons stack into successive shells rather than collapsing together — the foundation of atomic structure, chemistry, and the very solidity of matter.
depths.deep: The deep 'spin–statistics' connection — that fermions are antisymmetric and bosons symmetric when two are swapped — can only be proven within relativistic quantum field theory. A striking consequence: 'electron degeneracy pressure,' a purely quantum push arising from exclusion, is what holds up white dwarf stars (and, with neutrons, neutron stars) against their own crushing gravity.

atoms.note: Fermions (half-integer spin) refuse to share states; bosons (integer spin) happily pile up — the basis of all matter structure.
atoms.art_prompt: atomic orbitals filling with up/down spin arrows, one electron per state, building shells like rungs forced apart

quiz.prompt: What does the Pauli exclusion principle forbid, and to which particles does it apply?
quiz.answer: It forbids two identical fermions (half-integer-spin particles) from occupying the same quantum state.

quiz.prompt: How does spin and exclusion explain the structure of the periodic table?
quiz.answer: Electrons are spin-½ fermions; exclusion forces them into successively higher energy shells rather than all collapsing to the lowest, producing the layered electron configurations behind chemical periodicity.

atoms.title: The hydrogen atom and quantized energy levels
atoms.summary: Solving Schrödinger's equation for the Coulomb potential yields discrete energy levels and the shapes of atomic orbitals.

depths.eli5: A hydrogen atom is one electron bound to one proton. That electron can't have just any energy — only certain specific values, like standing on the steps of a staircase rather than anywhere on a ramp. When the electron jumps from one step to another, it emits or absorbs a flash of light of one exact color.
depths.core: The hydrogen atom is the great early triumph of quantum mechanics. Feeding the electron's Coulomb attraction to the proton (a potential energy that varies as 1/r, where r is the distance) into the Schrödinger equation gives bound-state energies E_n = −13.6 eV/n² (here 'eV,' electron-volt, is a tiny energy unit, and n = 1, 2, 3, … labels the levels). The solutions — the orbital wavefunctions or 'orbitals' — are labeled by three 'quantum numbers' (n, l, m), integers that fix the energy, shape, and orientation. Electrons jumping between these levels produce the sharp, specific 'spectral lines' (exact colors) we actually observe from glowing hydrogen.
depths.deep: The three quantum numbers fall out naturally when the equation is separated in spherical coordinates; l and m come specifically from the angular momentum operators. Adding the electron's spin and small relativistic corrections splits the levels slightly into 'fine structure.' The same framework generalizes (approximately) to every other atom, underpinning the entire periodic table of elements.

atoms.note: 13.6 eV is the ionization energy of hydrogen — the energy needed to rip its single electron entirely free.

quiz.prompt: What is the energy of the nth hydrogen level, and what does n = 1 give?
quiz.answer: E_n = −13.6 eV/n²; the ground state (n = 1) is −13.6 eV, the ionization energy.

quiz.prompt: Why does hydrogen emit light only at sharp, specific wavelengths?
quiz.answer: Because its energy levels are discrete; an electron dropping from one level to another emits a photon of energy exactly equal to the gap, giving precise spectral lines.

atoms.title: Entanglement and Bell's theorem
atoms.summary: Two particles can share a single quantum state with correlations no local classical theory can reproduce.

depths.eli5: Two particles can be linked — 'entangled' — so that measuring one instantly tells you something about the other, even if they're far apart. The catch: the coordination between them is too strong to be explained by them having secretly 'agreed on the answers' before separating. Reality is genuinely stranger than that.
depths.core: In an 'entangled' state, the pair as a whole has a complete description, but neither particle alone does. Measuring one particle's spin instantly fixes the probability of its partner's outcome, no matter how far apart they are. A 'local hidden-variable theory' is the common-sense idea that the particles carried predetermined answers all along. Bell's theorem proves that the correlations quantum mechanics predicts are stronger than any such theory can produce — and real experiments confirm the quantum prediction, ruling out that comforting picture ('local realism').
depths.deep: Crucially, entanglement cannot send a usable message faster than light: each individual outcome is random, so no controllable signal travels — relativity is safe. Yet it definitively rules out local realism. Far from a paradox, entanglement is now a practical resource: it is the engine behind quantum computing, quantum teleportation, and quantum cryptography.

atoms.note: Entanglement correlates outcomes but cannot transmit a signal — so there is no conflict with relativity's speed limit.
atoms.art_prompt: two distant detectors measuring a shared singlet pair, anti-correlated spin readings linked by a glowing nonlocal connection

quiz.prompt: What does Bell's theorem establish about quantum correlations?
quiz.answer: That entangled-particle correlations exceed what any local hidden-variable (local-realist) theory can produce, ruling out local realism.

quiz.prompt: Explain why entanglement does not violate relativity despite its 'instant' correlation.
quiz.answer: The measurement outcome on each side is random; no controllable information is transmitted, so no signal travels faster than light.

atoms.title: Quantum field theory — the idea
atoms.summary: Particles are quantized excitations of underlying fields that fill all of space — the marriage of quantum mechanics and special relativity.

depths.eli5: Go deep enough and the most fundamental things aren't particles at all — they're invisible 'fields' that fill all of space. What we call a 'particle' is just a ripple, a localized vibration, in one of those fields. And ripples can be created or destroyed, which is why particles can pop into and out of existence.
depths.core: A 'field' is something with a value at every point in space (like the electric field you already met). Quantum field theory (QFT) promotes fields — not particles — to the most fundamental objects. Each kind of particle is a 'quantized field' whose ripples (excitations) are the particles; for example, the photon is a single quantum of the electromagnetic field. QFT becomes necessary because combining quantum mechanics with special relativity allows particles to be created and destroyed (since E = mc² lets pure energy turn into new mass).
depths.deep: The fields obey 'commutation' relations for bosons or 'anticommutation' relations for fermions — and this is finally where the spin–statistics connection and the Pauli exclusion principle get rigorously proven. Interactions are calculated step by step ('perturbatively') using Feynman diagrams (pictures standing for terms in the math), and a procedure called 'renormalization' tames the infinities that appear. QFT is the most precisely tested framework in all of science.

atoms.note: The photon is the quantum (single ripple) of the electromagnetic field — QFT is why 'particle' and 'wave' finally stop being a paradox.

quiz.prompt: In quantum field theory, what is a particle?
quiz.answer: A quantized excitation (a ripple) of an underlying field that pervades all of space.

quiz.prompt: Why is a field theory needed when relativity meets quantum mechanics?
quiz.answer: Relativity's E = mc² permits energy to create and destroy particles, so a fixed-particle wavefunction is inadequate; a field describing variable particle number is required.

atoms.title: The Standard Model (a glimpse)
atoms.summary: All known matter and three of the four forces are described by quantized fields with a precise gauge symmetry.

depths.eli5: Everything in the universe is built from a surprisingly small set of building-block particles (called quarks and leptons). They're held together by 'force-carrier' particles that ferry the forces between them. And one special field, the Higgs, is what gives many of these particles their mass.
depths.core: The Standard Model is the quantum field theory of all known matter and three of the four forces. The matter particles are six 'quarks' (which make up protons and neutrons) and six 'leptons' (the electron and its relatives). They interact by exchanging 'force carriers': gluons (the strong force, gluing nuclei together), the W and Z particles (the weak force, behind some radioactivity), and the photon (electromagnetism). The whole structure is dictated by a 'gauge symmetry' labeled SU(3)×SU(2)×U(1) — a deep mathematical symmetry that forces each force to exist. The Higgs field, whose particle was confirmed in 2012, gives particles mass through a process called symmetry breaking.
depths.deep: Its predictions match experiment to staggering precision, yet it is incomplete: it leaves out gravity entirely, says nothing about dark matter, doesn't explain why neutrinos have mass, and can't account for why the universe has far more matter than antimatter. The guiding idea — 'gauge symmetry,' demanding the laws stay unchanged under certain local transformations — is what dictates the existence and exact form of every force in the model.

atoms.note: It excludes gravity; unifying the Standard Model with general relativity (a 'theory of everything') remains one of physics' biggest open problems.

quiz.answer: Gravity; the Standard Model covers the electromagnetic, weak, and strong forces but not gravitation.

atoms.title: Expanding universe (a glimpse)
atoms.summary: Applying general relativity to the whole cosmos yields an expanding universe with a hot, dense origin.

depths.eli5: The entire universe is stretching, like the surface of a balloon being inflated. Distant galaxies are rushing away from us, and the farther one is, the faster it recedes. Run that stretching backward in your mind and everything was once squeezed into an incredibly hot, tiny beginning — the Big Bang.
depths.core: Hubble's law, v = H₀d, says a galaxy's recession speed v grows in proportion to its distance d (H₀ is Hubble's constant) — exactly the pattern you'd see if all of space is uniformly expanding. The Friedmann equations — Einstein's field equation applied to a uniform, even universe — describe how the 'scale factor' a(t) (a number tracking the overall size of space over time) changes as the cosmic energy density ρ evolves. Running this backward leads to a hot, dense origin (the Big Bang), whose leftover glow we still detect today as the cosmic microwave background (CMB).
depths.deep: Careful observations show the expansion is actually accelerating, blamed on 'dark energy' — often modeled as Einstein's cosmological constant Λ. Meanwhile most of the matter is invisible 'dark matter,' known only by its gravity. The cosmic energy budget — a few percent ordinary matter, more dark matter, and a majority dark energy — is one of the deepest unsolved puzzles in all of physics.

atoms.note: The cosmic microwave background is the relic light released when the cooling universe first became transparent, about 380,000 years after the Big Bang.
atoms.art_prompt: galaxies on an expanding grid all receding from each other, redshifted light stretching, traced back to a hot dense origin

quiz.prompt: What does Hubble's law relate, and what does it imply about the universe?
quiz.answer: Recession velocity to distance (v = H₀d); it implies the universe is uniformly expanding.

quiz.prompt: What observation is taken as direct evidence of a hot early universe?
quiz.answer: The cosmic microwave background — relic thermal radiation left over from when the universe cooled enough to become transparent.

atoms.title: Contact forces and friction
atoms.summary: Surfaces resist sliding with a friction force proportional to how hard they are pressed together.

depths.eli5: Two surfaces touching grip each other and resist sliding — that resistance is friction. The harder you press the surfaces together, the harder they grip and the more they resist sliding. Push gently and nothing moves; push hard enough and the grip suddenly gives way and they slide.
depths.core: There are two kinds. 'Static friction' acts while things aren't yet sliding and can adjust itself up to a maximum of μ_s·N to exactly cancel whatever push you apply (μ_s, 'mu-s', is the static friction coefficient). 'Kinetic friction' acts once sliding has started: f_k = μ_k·N, a roughly steady drag, where μ_k is usually a bit smaller than μ_s (so things are easier to keep moving than to start). The 'normal force' N is the surface's perpendicular push back on the object. These simple, experimentally-found rules let everyday mechanics problems be solved with 'free-body diagrams' (sketches of all the forces on an object).
depths.deep: Friction isn't a fundamental force — it emerges from countless electromagnetic interactions between surface atoms plus microscopic roughness. It converts ordered mechanical energy into disordered heat, which is why frictional processes can't be run backward (they're irreversible) and tie directly back to the second law of thermodynamics.

atoms.note: Static friction is a range (anything up to μ_s N), not a fixed value — it rises to match whatever force you apply, right up until the surface slips.

quiz.answer: Kinetic friction is f_k = μ_k N (fixed once sliding); static friction can take any value up to a maximum μ_s N to prevent motion.

quiz.answer: Friction converts ordered mechanical energy into disordered heat, an irreversible dissipation that increases entropy — the second law in everyday form.

atoms.title: Fluid flow and Bernoulli's principle
atoms.summary: In steady flow, faster-moving fluid has lower pressure — energy conservation written for fluids.

depths.eli5: Here's a surprising rule about moving liquids and gases (together called fluids): where a fluid flows faster, its pressure actually drops. That's a big part of why fast-moving air over the curved top of an airplane wing creates lower pressure there and helps lift the plane.
depths.core: A 'streamline' is the path a small parcel of fluid follows. Bernoulli's equation is conservation of energy written per unit volume along a streamline, for an 'ideal' fluid (incompressible — it doesn't squish — and non-viscous — no internal stickiness): the sum of pressure P, kinetic energy ½ρv² (ρ, 'rho', is density), and gravitational term ρgh stays constant. Paired with the 'continuity' rule (cross-sectional area × speed = constant, so flow speeds up in narrow spots), it explains aircraft lift, venturi meters (flow gauges), and why pinching a hose makes water shoot faster.
depths.deep: It assumes no viscosity and smooth, steady, non-swirling ('irrotational') flow — real fluids deviate through drag and turbulence, governed by the far harder Navier–Stokes equations. At root, Bernoulli's principle is just the work–energy theorem (an earlier atom) applied to a moving parcel of fluid.

atoms.art_prompt: fluid streamlines crowding through a pipe constriction, speeding up where pressure gauges read lower

quiz.prompt: What does Bernoulli's principle say about the pressure of a faster-moving fluid?
quiz.answer: Its pressure is lower; pressure plus kinetic plus gravitational energy per volume is constant along a streamline.

quiz.prompt: Why does air flowing faster over the top of a wing contribute to lift?
quiz.answer: Faster flow over the top means lower pressure there; the higher pressure below pushes the wing upward.

atoms.title: Heat engines and the Carnot limit
atoms.summary: No heat engine working between two temperatures can beat the Carnot efficiency set by their ratio.

depths.eli5: An engine turns heat into useful work — but it can never turn ALL the heat into work. It always has to throw some heat away to a cooler side. The bigger the temperature difference between the hot source and the cold dump, the more useful work you can squeeze out.
depths.core: A 'heat engine' takes in heat from a hot 'reservoir' (a large heat source at temperature T_h), converts part of it to work, and dumps the rest to a cold reservoir (T_c). The second law of thermodynamics caps the efficiency (work out divided by heat in) at the 'Carnot' value 1 − T_c/T_h — reachable only by a perfect, infinitely slow 'reversible' cycle. Real engines always fall short because of friction, fast heat transfer, and other 'irreversibilities' that generate extra entropy.
depths.deep: Carnot's remarkable result doesn't depend on what the engine is made of or what fuel it burns — only on the two reservoir temperatures. That universality is precisely what lets the absolute (Kelvin) temperature scale be defined thermodynamically, through engine efficiency itself.

atoms.note: Carnot efficiency depends only on the two temperatures, never on the engine's design, materials, or fuel.
atoms.art_prompt: a cyclic engine pulling heat from a hot reservoir, outputting work, and dumping the remainder to a cold reservoir, efficiency capped by the temperature ratio

quiz.prompt: Write the maximum (Carnot) efficiency of a heat engine between temperatures T_h and T_c.
quiz.answer: η_Carnot = 1 − T_c/T_h, achievable only by a reversible engine.

quiz.prompt: Why can no engine ever reach 100% efficiency converting heat to work?
quiz.answer: Rejecting some heat to a cold reservoir is required to keep total entropy from decreasing; reaching 100% would demand T_c = 0 or violate the second law.

atoms.title: Electric potential and capacitance
atoms.summary: Electric potential is potential energy per unit charge; capacitors store charge and energy by holding a voltage across a gap.

depths.eli5: Voltage is like electrical 'height': charges roll 'downhill' from high voltage to low, the way a ball rolls down a slope. A capacitor is essentially a tiny bucket that stores up electric charge when you push a voltage across its two plates, and releases it later.
depths.core: 'Electric potential' V (measured in volts) is electric potential energy per unit charge — how much energy each unit of charge carries at a given spot. The field relates to it by E = −∇V (the field points downhill in voltage, toward lower potential). Because Coulomb forces are conservative, V depends only on location, not on the path taken to get there. A 'capacitor' is two conductors that store opposite charges; the charge stored Q is proportional to the applied voltage V, with the proportionality constant C called 'capacitance.' A charged capacitor holds energy ½CV² in the electric field between its plates.
depths.deep: 'Equipotential surfaces' (sets of points at the same voltage) are always perpendicular to the field lines, and any conductor in static equilibrium is itself one big equipotential. The stored energy ½CV² genuinely lives in the electric field itself (the energy density is proportional to E²) — an early hint that fields are physically real carriers of energy, not just bookkeeping.

atoms.note: Voltage is energy per unit charge; the field points from high to low potential (E = −∇V).

quiz.prompt: How are electric field and electric potential related?
quiz.answer: The field is minus the gradient of the potential, E = −∇V; the field points toward decreasing potential.

atoms.title: Circuits — Ohm's law and Kirchhoff's rules
atoms.summary: Current, voltage, and resistance obey simple linear and conservation rules that solve any DC circuit.

depths.eli5: Think of an electric circuit like water in pipes. Voltage is the push, current is the flow, and resistance is how much the pipe fights the flow. Two common-sense rules hold: water (charge) is never lost where pipes meet, and if you walk all the way around any loop you end up back at the same height (voltage).
depths.core: 'Current' I is the rate of charge flow; 'resistance' R measures how much a component opposes it. Ohm's law, V = IR, relates the voltage across a resistor to the current through it. Kirchhoff's two rules let you solve any direct-current (DC) circuit: the 'junction rule' (charge conservation — all current flowing into a junction equals all flowing out) and the 'loop rule' (energy conservation — the voltage changes around any closed loop add up to zero). Together they handle arbitrarily tangled resistor networks.
depths.deep: Kirchhoff's rules are simply charge conservation and energy conservation dressed up in circuit language. Ohm's law, by contrast, is empirical, not a fundamental law — it holds for 'ohmic' materials where the charges' average drift speed is proportional to the field. Many useful devices (diodes, transistors) are deliberately 'non-ohmic,' and that nonlinearity is exactly what makes electronics possible.

atoms.note: Junction rule = conservation of charge; loop rule = conservation of energy — both in circuit clothing.

quiz.prompt: State Kirchhoff's two rules and the conservation law each expresses.
quiz.answer: Junction rule: currents into a node equal currents out (charge conservation). Loop rule: voltage changes around any closed loop sum to zero (energy conservation).

quiz.prompt: Two resistors R₁ and R₂ are in series across voltage V. What current flows?
quiz.answer: The same current through both, I = V/(R₁ + R₂), since series resistances add.

atoms.title: Blackbody radiation and Planck's law
atoms.summary: The thermal glow of a hot body required energy to be quantized — the birth of quantum theory.

depths.eli5: Hot things glow, and the color of the glow tells you the temperature — think of metal going from red-hot to white-hot as it heats. Explaining the exact mix of colors in that glow turned out to be impossible with old physics, and fixing it forced scientists to admit, for the first time, that light energy comes in tiny chunks.
depths.core: A 'blackbody' is an idealized object that perfectly absorbs and re-emits radiation; its glow depends only on temperature. Classical physics disastrously predicted that a blackbody would radiate infinite energy at short wavelengths — the famous 'ultraviolet catastrophe.' In 1900 Max Planck fixed it by assuming the little oscillators emitting the light could only carry energy in whole multiples of hν (h is Planck's constant, ν the frequency). That single 'quantization' assumption produced exactly the right spectrum — and unintentionally launched all of quantum mechanics.
depths.deep: Planck's law contains two earlier rules as special cases: Wien's displacement law (the glow's peak color shifts toward blue as temperature rises) and the Stefan–Boltzmann law (total emitted power grows as T⁴). The cosmic microwave background — the relic glow of the Big Bang — is a near-perfect blackbody spectrum, making this curve one of the most precisely measured in all of nature.

atoms.note: Planck introduced energy quantization reluctantly, as a mathematical trick to fit the data — it turned out to be how the world actually works.
atoms.art_prompt: blackbody spectral curves at several temperatures, peaks shifting toward blue as it heats, contrasted with the runaway classical prediction

quiz.prompt: What assumption did Planck introduce to explain blackbody radiation?
quiz.answer: That the emitting oscillators could only carry energy in discrete quanta of size hν — energy quantization.

quiz.prompt: What was the 'ultraviolet catastrophe' and how did quantization resolve it?
quiz.answer: Classical theory predicted infinite emission at short wavelengths; quantizing energy makes high-frequency modes exponentially suppressed, giving a finite, correct spectrum.

atoms.title: Bohr model of the atom
atoms.summary: Quantizing electron angular momentum produced the first correct atomic spectra, bridging to full quantum mechanics.

depths.eli5: Before the full theory existed, Niels Bohr made a bold guess: electrons can only circle the nucleus at certain special distances, not just any. When an electron hops from one allowed orbit to another, it gives off light of one exact color. Amazingly, the guess matched the real colors hydrogen emits.
depths.core: Bohr postulated that only orbits with angular momentum equal to a whole number times ℏ are stable (L = nℏ, n = 1, 2, 3, …), and that light is emitted or absorbed when an electron jumps between orbits, with the photon energy hf equal to the energy gap between them (f is the light's frequency). This neatly reproduced hydrogen's spectral lines and the 13.6 eV energy scale. It was a 'semi-classical' patch — part old physics, part quantum guess — later fully superseded by Schrödinger's wave mechanics.
depths.deep: Bohr's rule L = nℏ turns out to be exactly the condition that a whole number of de Broglie matter-wavelengths fit around the orbit — a strong hint that the real story is wave-like, not little planets on tracks. The proper Schrödinger treatment of hydrogen recovers Bohr's energy levels while replacing his definite orbits with fuzzy probability clouds (orbitals).

atoms.note: Bohr's neat orbits are a useful fiction — full quantum mechanics replaces them with three-dimensional probability clouds.

quiz.prompt: What quantity did Bohr quantize, and what determines the frequency of emitted light?
quiz.answer: He quantized orbital angular momentum (L = nℏ); emitted light has hf equal to the energy difference between two levels.

quiz.answer: Requiring a whole number of de Broglie wavelengths to fit around an orbit gives exactly L = nℏ, recasting the rule as a standing-wave condition.

atoms.title: Quantum harmonic oscillator
atoms.summary: A quantum oscillator has equally spaced energy levels and a nonzero ground-state energy even at absolute zero.

depths.eli5: Take the back-and-forth wobble of a spring (simple harmonic motion) into the quantum world. Now the wobbling system can only hold certain specific amounts of energy — evenly spaced steps. And it can never be perfectly still: even at the lowest possible energy, it always jiggles a tiny bit.
depths.core: A 'quadratic potential' is the energy bowl of a spring (energy grows as displacement squared). Solving the Schrödinger equation for it gives evenly spaced energy levels E_n = ℏω(n + ½), where ω is the classical wobble frequency and n = 0, 1, 2, … The crucial '½' is the 'zero-point energy': even the lowest state (n = 0) has energy, because the uncertainty principle forbids a particle from having both exactly zero position and exactly zero momentum at once. This model underlies molecular vibrations, 'phonons' (quantized sound vibrations in solids), and quantized fields.
depths.deep: The quantum oscillator is one of the few problems solved exactly, using elegant 'raising and lowering' (creation/annihilation) operators — the very same algebra later used to quantize fields in quantum field theory. Its universality (any smooth potential minimum looks harmonic up close, as noted in the classical SHM atom) makes it the workhorse model of all quantum physics.

atoms.note: Zero-point energy ½ℏω is real and measurable — it keeps helium liquid even at absolute zero and produces the Casimir effect (a tiny force between nearby plates in vacuum).
atoms.art_prompt: a parabolic potential well with evenly spaced energy rungs and a lowest level sitting above the bottom, its wavefunction never reaching zero spread

quiz.prompt: What is the energy spectrum of the quantum harmonic oscillator?
quiz.answer: E_n = ℏω(n + ½) for n = 0, 1, 2, …; levels are equally spaced by ℏω with a ½ℏω zero-point offset.

quiz.prompt: Why does the quantum oscillator have nonzero energy in its ground state?
quiz.answer: The uncertainty principle forbids simultaneously definite zero position and zero momentum, so the lowest state retains zero-point energy ½ℏω.
